content: No research evidence has been identified regarding the impact of insurance reforms that equalize physician fees for vaginal births and cesarean sections on equity. This is particularly relevant in settings where increased physician fees are not covered by government or national health insurance programs, potentially leading to financial barriers for households unable to afford high physician fees. Additionally, no research evidence has been identified on other considerations, such as cost-effectiveness or acceptability, for financial strategies. As a result, the effects of these financial strategies on outcomes remain uncertain, and further research is needed to explore these issues. Insurance reforms that equalize physician fees for vaginal births and cesarean sections, compared to usual practice, have uncertain desirable effects due to the lack of included studies. The certainty of evidence for desirable effects is very low, and the undesirable effects are also uncertain, as they have not been assessed in included studies. The balance of effects is unclear, with varying judgments on whether these reforms favor usual practice or equalized fees. There is important uncertainty or variability in values, and the required resources for implementation are also uncertain, with potential costs ranging from negligible to large. The cost-effectiveness of these reforms is similarly uncertain, with no clear evidence favoring either usual practice or equalized fees. Equity impacts are unknown, and acceptability and feasibility vary depending on the context. Several barriers may hinder the effective implementation and scaling up of the recommendations in this guideline. These barriers may relate to the behaviors of patients (women or families), healthcare professionals, the organization of care, health service delivery, or financial arrangements. Strategies to address these barriers include community-level sensitization activities to disseminate information about the risks of unnecessary cesarean sections and the benefits of adhering to recommended practices, involving local opinion leaders and champions to promote implementation, and providing education to healthcare professionals to integrate recommended behaviors into their practice. Training institutions and professional bodies should be involved to update pre-service and in-service training curricula with the recommendations. Successful implementation strategies should be documented and shared as examples for other implementers. Local, case-specific protocols should be developed to ensure timely and appropriate senior clinician review for cesarean section indications. The implementation and impact of the recommendations can be monitored at health service, regional, and country levels using clearly defined criteria and indicators associated with locally agreed targets. WHO standards for improving the quality of maternal and newborn care in health facilities provide prioritized input, output, and outcome measures that can be used to define quality-of-care criteria and indicators. Data on countryand regional-level implementation of the recommendations will be collected to evaluate their impact on national policies of individual WHO Member States. Future research should address the uncertainty in the effects of interventions due to very low or low certainty evidence, concerns about the applicability of evidence (as most interventions were assessed in single studies), and the lack of studies for predefined guideline questions. Research should also focus on locally relevant determinants of cesarean births through formative studies. Pragmatic randomized controlled trials or cluster-randomized trials are encouraged, with sufficient sample sizes to assess intervention effects by factors such as parity, socioeconomic status, staffing patterns, practice settings, and geographical regions. Mixed-methods studies integrating quantitative and qualitative data are recommended to provide insights into the effects of interventions. Interventions should be multifaceted and tailored to local determinants of cesarean section practices. Educational interventions targeted at women, such as birth preparation classes, psychoeducation by telephone, and prenatal education for partners, should be explored. Interventions targeting healthcare professionals, such as audit and feedback using the Robson classification, and those targeting health organizations, such as insurance reforms equalizing physician fees, collaborative midwifery-obstetrician care models, and midwife-led continuity models of care, should also be studied further. Additional research is needed to confirm observed benefits in reducing cesarean births in areas with high cesarean section rates. Studies should fully describe intervention components to facilitate implementation and replication. The use of the Template for Intervention Description and Replication (TIDieR) checklist is recommended. A unified system for classifying and reporting cesarean sections should be developed to improve the synthesis and interpretation of findings across studies. A comprehensive typology of interventions to reduce cesarean sections should be created to aid categorization, comparison, and synthesis in systematic reviews and related research.
